question: What process does Jason Lemkin recommend for balancing sales feature requests against product priorities without repeatedly disrupting engineering?
expected_points: Give sales a defined feature-request budget each quarter and let its leader prioritize within it.
Review requests regularly with sales, including what is planned for upcoming quarters.
Explain that changing committed work has a high cost and becomes more disruptive later in the quarter.
evidence_quote: Every quarter, give your head of sales a certain budget, whether it's story points or 10% of the pie chart, however you do it, give them a budget.

answer.summary: Lemkin recommends giving sales a quarterly feature budget and reviewing it weekly with product, so sales can prioritize requests without constantly reshuffling engineering work. Changes to uncommitted plans are easier; disrupting work already underway should be treated as a deliberate, exceptional tradeoff.

sections.heading: A process for handling requests (synthesis)
sections.content: Set a fixed budget for sales each quarter—such as story points or 10% of the roadmap—and have the VP of Sales load-balance requests across the year rather than letting each urgent deal reset priorities. Hold a weekly meeting between the VPs of Sales and Product to review the budget and requests. Sales should force-rank requests with its team first; Lemkin says those rankings often look different after the discussion. In the weekly review, show what is being built for sales and what is planned for the next two quarters, and ask whether sales wants to change the uncommitted plans.

sections.heading: Protect work in progress and clarify decision-making
sections.content: Make the cost of a change explicit: changing priorities before code is committed is an option, but dropping or shelving work already underway is “hyper disruptive.” Lemkin gives the example of an integration that is 80% complete; a startup might shelve it for a million-dollar deal, but should confirm that sales truly wants that tradeoff. If an individual salesperson asks a PM to add a feature, the PM should route the request through the appropriate managers rather than treating the salesperson’s request as a decision. Lemkin says some tension between sales and product is healthy, provided there is enough process to keep it from damaging the organization.

sections.content: Each quarter, give the head of Sales a defined allocation—such as story points or 10% of the roadmap. Have Sales surface and force-rank requests; Lemkin says this often changes what the team prioritizes once people compare requests together. The Sales leader can then balance requests across the year instead of letting each urgent deal reset the roadmap.

sections.content: Have the VP of Sales and VP of Product meet weekly to review the budget and priorities. Show Sales what is being built for its allocation and what is planned for the next two quarters, and ask whether it wants to change future priorities. A junior salesperson bringing a request to a PM should generally hear, “I will talk to my boss”; the issue should be escalated through the leaders’ process rather than decided ad hoc.

answer.summary: Lemkin recommends giving sales a fixed quarterly feature budget, having sales rank and balance requests within it, and reviewing priorities weekly with product. Keep near-term work visible and change committed work only after making the disruption explicit. [S1, S2, S3, S4]

sections.heading: Set a quarterly sales budget
sections.content: Give the head of sales a defined amount of product capacity each quarter—for example, story points or 10% of the available work. Lemkin’s rationale is that customers tend to think in quarterly or larger release cycles, even if teams ship more often. [S1]

sections.heading: Make sales prioritize its own requests
sections.content: Ask sales to force-rank requests across the team and load-balance them over the year, rather than treating each new deal as an automatic roadmap change. Lemkin says the ranking can change substantially once the team discusses and compares requests. [S2, S3]

sections.heading: Review the budget and roadmap weekly
sections.content: Have the VP of Sales and VP of Product meet weekly about the budget, with sales surfacing and ranking its requests. Show what is being built now and what is planned for the next two quarters; invite sales to change uncommitted plans before code is committed. If a PM is not empowered to decide, Lemkin says the right response is to take the request to their manager. [S2, S3, S5]

sections.heading: Make exceptions explicit
sections.content: A major deal can justify changing work in progress, but state the tradeoff plainly—for example, that shelving an integration that is already 80% complete to pursue a million-dollar deal will disrupt the organization. Lemkin advises against emotional, repeated pivots: involve sales as a stakeholder and let them knowingly choose whether the deal warrants the disruption. This process is a synthesis of his recommendations, not a guarantee that disruption can always be avoided. [S4]
